subtype: Approach: scenario plan if the money is late [Thinking]
passage:
Devika's office had lost power an hour ago, so she sat by a torch on the floor of the empty workshop, a notebook on her knee and the payroll date six weeks away. Her co-founder Urmila leaned on the door frame.
"Everyone tells me the round takes longer than promised," Devika said, tapping the page. "Usually about double. So I won't plan on one future. Case one: money arrives by month three. We keep the hiring plan. Case two: month six. We pause the extra hire and move to a smaller room. Case three: it never comes. Then we keep the core team and live off customers only."
"And the cuts for each?"
"Written beside each case, so nobody argues about them when the day comes."
Urmila nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where was Devika sitting while she wrote the three cases?
qa.a: Devika was sitting on the floor of the empty workshop by a torch.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as she wrote out the three cases?
qa.a: Devika was anxious but steady, focused on preparing rather than hoping, which is why she wrote the cuts next to each case.

qa.q: What could Devika do next to check whether case three is workable?
qa.a: Devika could ask a few customers whether they would keep paying if the team shrank, and test the customer-only plan with real numbers.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt seeing the three cases?
qa.a: Urmila was probably reassured, because even the worst case had a written plan, which her slow nod suggests.

grounding: The passage shows a founder who expects a funding round to run late and prepares three cases with matching cost cuts for each.

subtype: Approach: scenario plan if the money is late [Thinking]
passage:
Mahima's investor meetings in Bengaluru were going well, and everyone kept saying, "We'll close in six weeks." Her mentor, Hansa, laughed when she heard. "Everyone says six weeks. Plan for six months. And plan for never."
That night in her Koramangala flat, Mahima opened a blank sheet and made three columns.
Case A: money arrives in three months. Hire two engineers in April as planned.
Case B: money arrives in six months. Freeze hiring; she and her co-founder take half salaries from May; drop the paid design tool.
Case C: no money at all. By July, shrink to the two founders and one support person, move to a cheaper co-working seat, and focus only on paying customers.
Beside each case she wrote the date on which she would switch. When April came with only "positive noises" from investors, she didn't panic. She moved to Case B that Monday.

qa.q: What would they do in Case B?
qa.a: Freeze hiring, take half salaries from May and drop the paid design tool.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when April came with only positive noises?
qa.a: She stayed calm instead of panicking, because the switch to Case B was already planned.

qa.q: What else could strengthen Mahima's plan?
qa.a: Sharing the three cases with her co-founder and team early, so any switch doesn't come as a shock.

qa.q: How does Hansa see promises of closing in six weeks?
qa.a: Hansa is sceptical, having seen rounds take far longer, and laughs at the usual six weeks.

grounding: It shows a founder expecting a round to take longer than promised and preparing three cases, funded in three months, in six or never, each with matching cuts.

subtype: Approach: scenario plan if the money is late [Thinking]
passage:
"The investors say they'll close by March," Ramesh said, hopeful.
"They said December, two months ago," Keerthana replied. "Rounds always drag on for double whatever anyone promises. So let's plan three ways."
"Three?"
"One: the money comes in three months. We hire as planned. Two: it comes in six months. We don't hire, we delay the office move, and we both take less salary from April. Three: it never comes."
"Don't say that."
"I'm saying it so we're ready. If it never comes, we cut to just us and the two support staff by June and chase only paying customers."
"And when do we decide which one we're in?"
"We write the dates now. If nothing's signed by 1 April, we're in case two. By 1 July, case three."
Ramesh exhaled. "Strangely, that makes me less scared."

qa.q: By what date would they be in case two?
qa.a: If nothing is signed by 1 April.

qa.q: Why does Ramesh feel less scared with the plan?
qa.a: Ramesh feels less scared because every outcome now has a ready response and a clear switch date.

qa.q: What makes writing the dates now useful?
qa.a: It removes the temptation to keep hoping and delaying; the decision is made calmly in advance.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see the investors' promise to close by March?
qa.a: Keerthana is sceptical, since they promised December two months ago.

grounding: It shows co-founders assuming the round may take twice as long and planning three cases, funded in three months, in six or not at all, with cuts for each.
